Consequently, returning after the unified-storage write can immediately cancel the legacy write, even though its ten-second timeout has not elapsed. This makes successful requests routinely leave legacy storage unsynchronized. Preserve the request's context values while detaching cancellation, then apply the background timeout."

For PATCH and server-side apply, UpdatedObjectInfo computes the update from the old object supplied by the store. Legacy storage can have a different or stale old object, so replaying the update can preserve stale fields or produce a different result from the successful unified update. Even a client that waits for a create response before deleting can have the legacy delete run before the pending legacy create. The delete then returns NotFound, its error is ignored, and the late create leaves a legacy object that no longer exists in unified storage. Sequential updates can likewise overwrite newer legacy state with older state. Background replication needs per-resource ordering or an equivalent version-aware mechanism."

findings.title: Detach background writes from request cancellation
findings.body: All four background writes derive their timeout context from the original request context. WithTimeoutCause preserves parent cancellation, and an HTTP request's context is canceled when its handler returns. Consequently, returning after the unified-storage write can immediately cancel the legacy write, even though its ten-second timeout has not elapsed. This makes successful requests routinely leave legacy storage unsynchronized. Preserve the request's context values while detaching cancellation, then apply the background timeout.

findings.title: Replicate the committed update instead of replaying objInfo
findings.body: The legacy update now receives the original UpdatedObjectInfo instead of a wrapper containing the object committed to unified storage. For PATCH and server-side apply, UpdatedObjectInfo computes the update from the old object supplied by the store. Legacy storage can have a different or stale old object, so replaying the update can preserve stale fields or produce a different result from the successful unified update. Restore replication of the committed result rather than independently evaluating the request against legacy state.

findings.title: Preserve operation ordering in asynchronous legacy writes
findings.body: Each write launches an independent goroutine, with no ordering between operations on the same resource. Even a client that waits for a create response before deleting can have the legacy delete run before the pending legacy create. The delete then returns NotFound, its error is ignored, and the late create leaves a legacy object that no longer exists in unified storage. Sequential updates can likewise overwrite newer legacy state with older state. Background replication needs per-resource ordering or an equivalent version-aware mechanism.

findings.title: Attribute duration metrics to the backend that performed the operation
findings.body: The unified-storage Create failure is recorded with recordLegacyDuration, although no legacy operation ran. Update has the same mistake at line 129. Conversely, the background legacy DeleteCollection call records recordStorageDuration at line 166. These observations hide unified create/update failures, falsely report legacy failures, and mix legacy collection-delete latency and errors into unified-storage metrics. Use the corresponding backend's recorder at each call site.

findings.title: Do not use resource names as the kind metric label
findings.body: The successful Delete observation passes name in the argument used for options.Kind everywhere else, including this method's error path. Every deleted resource name therefore creates a distinct duration-metric label value instead of sharing the resource-kind value. Normal resource churn can create unbounded Prometheus series and memory usage, while successful and failed deletions cannot be aggregated under the same kind. Pass options.Kind here.

findings.title: Independently verify completion of legacy writes
findings.body: The new tests give legacy and unified storage the same mock, whose expectations use identical method names. A legacy expectation can therefore satisfy a unified call; the Create error case actually configures only setupLegacyFn yet exercises the unified failure path. The tests also neither await background writes nor assert their call counts, so deleting every legacy-write goroutine would still pass these unit tests. Use separate mocks and synchronize assertions on legacy completion to verify the central mode-3 replication behavior.
